title: Writing Effective Unit Tests
keywords: avoiding tests that merely duplicate implementation
subtopics: Avoiding tests that merely duplicate implementation.
learning_outcomes: Explain what writing effective unit tests contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: arrange, act, and assert.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Quality comes from several kinds of evidence: unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, coding standards, and repeatable CI. Tests should assert observable behavior and include important failure and boundary cases. In this lesson, focus on arrange, act, and assert; then compare it with testing deterministic logic. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use writing effective unit tests when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Quality comes from several kinds of evidence: unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, coding standards, and repeatable CI. Tests should assert observable behavior and include important failure and boundary cases. For writing effective unit tests, begin with arrange, act, and assert. Also distinguish testing deterministic logic; boundary cases; meaningful assertions. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: Arrange, act, and assert
items.text: Know when to use arrange, act, and assert, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Testing deterministic logic
items.text: Write an assertion about observable behavior and include a boundary or failure case; a passing command alone does not prove the requirement.

items.title: Boundary cases
items.text: Know when to use boundary cases, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Meaningful assertions
items.text: Write an assertion about observable behavior and include a boundary or failure case; a passing command alone does not prove the requirement.

items.title: Avoiding tests that merely duplicate implementation
items.text: Write an assertion about observable behavior and include a boundary or failure case; a passing command alone does not prove the requirement.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Writing Effective Unit Tests
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$required = ["status", "message"]; $response = ["status" => 200, "message" => "ok"];
echo count(array_intersect($required, array_keys($response))) . " fields matched" . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Test observable behavior, include boundary cases, and treat static analysis and coverage as evidence rather than proof.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for writing effective unit tests from top to bottom. Start by identifying arrange, act, and assert, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

The learner can explain its input, rule, and observable output.

hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.
Keep the example small enough that you can predict the output manually.
Test one normal case and one empty, invalid, or boundary case.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary inputs and failures can reveal defects that normal examples miss.
common_mistakes.fix: Add empty, invalid, boundary, and failure cases with meaningful assertions.

common_mistakes.why: Tests can become brittle and stop checking real behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer simple unit tests and focused integration tests at actual boundaries.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating coverage as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Executing a line does not guarantee its behavior was asserted.
common_mistakes.fix: Review assertions, relevant branches, edge cases, and regression risk.

summary: Writing Effective Unit Tests is one part of the PHP implementation workflow.
Prefer explicit behavior and testable examples over implicit assumptions.
Test observable behavior, include boundary cases, and treat static analysis and coverage as evidence rather than proof.
